{"result": {"title": "Madame Bovary", "author": "Gustave Flaubert", "year": 1856, "word_count": 117000, "text": "Part I, Chapter 1.

We were at prep when the headmaster came in, followed by a new boy not wearing school uniform and a porter carrying a large desk. Those who were sleeping woke up, and everyone stood as if caught off-guard in the middle of his work.

The headmaster motioned for us to sit down; then, turning to the form master, he said in a low voice, 'Monsieur Rameau, here is a boy I am confiding to you. He will enter the fifth form. If his conduct and his studies deserve it he will go up into the upper grade, as befits a boy of his age.'

The new boy, who had remained in the corner behind the door, where he could hardly be seen, was a country lad of about fifteen, taller than any of us. His hair was cut straight across his forehead like a village chorister's. He had an earnest, embarrassed look. Although he was not broad-shouldered, his short school jacket of green cloth with black buttons must have been tight about the armholes and showed at the opening of the cuffs some red wrists accustomed to the open air. His feet, in thick boots ill-polished and studded with nails, were crossed, and he held his cap on his knees. It was one of those composite head-dresses in which one may find some of the features of the bearskin, the shako, the bowler, the otter-skin cap, and the cotton nightcap, in a word, one of those pitiable creations whose dumb ugliness suggests the unreachable depths of imbecility.", "source": "library-service"}, "error": null}
